title: Emergy

definition.text: The total energy of one kind, usually sunlight, used directly and indirectly to make a product or service; a way of expressing differences in energy quality.

facts.text: It puts sunlight, fuel, electricity and human services on a common basis by expressing each in the solar energy needed to produce them, measured in solar emjoules (seJ).
Howard T. Odum, studying energy flow in ecosystems from the 1950s, argued that different energy sources cannot be added without converting them to a common measure of quality.
Odum's first formal statement came in 1973; David Scienceman proposed the name 'emergy' in 1986.
Emergy accounting draws a system diagram, builds a table of resource, labour and energy flows, converts each to emergy and sums them.
Its stated goal is an 'ecocentric' valuation that adds information rather than replacing economic values.
Critics call it an energy theory of value, find unequal calories absurd, say the sunlight behind oil cannot be measured objectively, and fault it for ignoring market values.

contested_note: Emergy has been controversial in ecology, thermodynamics and economics, with critics rejecting its basic premises.

definition.text: The emergy needed per unit of available energy produced; a measure of an energy form's quality.

facts.text: If 10,000 solar emjoules are needed to make a joule of wood, the wood's solar transformity is 10,000 seJ/J.
The solar transformity of sunlight absorbed by the Earth is 1.0 by definition.
Odum's 1975 table of 'energy quality factors' first stated the energy hierarchy principle: quality is measured by the energy used in transformations.

definition.text: Ratios from emergy accounting that judge how a process uses local, renewable and purchased resources.

facts.text: The emergy yield ratio (EYR) measures how much an investment lets a process exploit local resources.
The environmental loading ratio (ELR) compares non-renewable and imported emergy with renewable emergy and indicates stress on ecosystems.
The emergy sustainability index (ESI) is EYR divided by ELR.

title: Energy return on investment

definition.text: The ratio of usable energy delivered by an energy source to the energy spent to obtain it.

facts.text: If EROI is one or less, the source becomes a net energy sink and can no longer serve as an energy source.
A fuel or energy source needs an EROI of at least 3:1 to be viable as a major source.
Charles A. S. Hall popularised energy analysis; his 1984 paper on the cover of Science gave EROI its greatest exposure.
Only human-applied energy counts as invested: sunlight driving biofuel crops is left out.
When EROI of an economy's main energy sources falls, energy gets harder to obtain and its relative price may rise.
For US fossil fuel discovery the ratio fell from about 1000:1 in 1919 to only 5:1 in the 2010s.
Researchers disagree on how far back into the supply chain to count energy inputs, so they reach different numbers for the same source.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on how to measure energy inputs, and an IEA-endorsed method gives more favourable values for solar panels.

title: EROI of energy sources
article: Energy return on investment#Application to various technologies

definition.text: Estimates of energy return on investment for particular technologies, from oil shale to hydropower.

facts.text: Hydropower plants average about 110 when run for about 100 years; nuclear plants range from 20 to 81.
Refined fuel from conventional oil ranges from around 18 to 43, while oil shale is typically around 1.4–1.5.
Wind turbines average around 16 unbuffered and 4 buffered in the literature; operating turbines averaged 19.8 in 2018 data.
A 2015 review found mean harmonised EROIs between 8.7 and 34.2 for photovoltaic modules, with payback times of 1.0 to 4.1 years.

notes: Figures come from differing studies and boundary choices; the verifier should keep each with its source.

title: Net energy and payback time
article: Energy return on investment#Relationship to net energy gain

definition.text: Net energy is the amount of energy gained from a source after subtracting what was invested, while EROI expresses the same thing as a ratio.

facts.text: A process with an EROI of 5 yields a net energy gain of 4 units for each unit spent.
Break-even is an EROI of 1, or net gain of 0; the time to reach it is the energy payback time.

definition.text: The argument that a declining energy return on investment helps explain why complex societies collapse.

facts.text: Thomas Homer-Dixon argues falling EROI was one reason the Western Roman Empire collapsed in the fifth century CE.
Joseph Tainter suggests a diminishing EROI is a chief cause of the collapse of complex societies.
Some historians link humanity's growing use of outside energy to easily exploited, high-EROI sources.

title: Expanded EROI calculations
article: Energy return on investment#Additional EROI calculations

definition.text: Three wider ways of counting EROI: point of use, extended and societal.

facts.text: Point-of-use EROI adds the cost of refining and transporting the fuel, which lowers the result.
Extended EROI also adds the infrastructure needed to transport the refined energy.
Societal EROI sums the EROIs of all fuels a nation uses; it has never been fully calculated.

definition.text: For a storage device, the ratio of electricity stored over its lifetime to the embodied electricity needed to build it.

facts.text: Reported values include 10 for a vanadium redox battery, 704 for pumped hydro and 792 for compressed-air storage.
A Stanford team found that without pumped storage, pairing wind with today's batteries would not be worth the investment.

title: Energy cannibalism
article: Energy return on investment#EROI under rapid growth

definition.text: The effect where rapid growth of an energy industry consumes the energy of existing plants to build new ones, limiting how fast it can grow.

facts.text: It limits the growth rate of energy technologies when climate neutrality is demanded.
A solar breeder, a panel factory powered by its own panels, overcomes some of these problems.
